en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga,
Nissaggiya Section (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on the Pairs, 4.
The Training Rule on Indicating Something Else.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā was ill.
Then a certain lay follower approached the bhikkhunī Thullanandā; having approached, he said this to her:
"What is troubling you, noble lady? What should be brought for you?"
“I have need of ghee, friend.
Then that lay follower, having brought ghee worth a kahāpaṇa from the house of a certain shopkeeper, gave it to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
The bhikkhunī Thullanandā spoke thus:
“I have no need for ghee, friend;
I have need of oil.
Then that lay follower went to the shopkeeper; having approached him, he said this to the shopkeeper:
“Noble sir, we have no need for ghee, noble lady; we need oil.
Here, take the ghee; give me the oil.
“If we, noble sir, were to take back goods once sold, when would our goods ever be sold?”
“Ghee was purchased with ghee; bring the purchase-price for oil, and you shall take the oil.
Then that lay follower complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can the noble lady Thullanandā, having requested one thing, request another?”
The bhikkhunīs heard that lay follower censuring, disparaging, and complaining.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... [as before] ...they censured, disparaged, and complained...
Then those bhikkhunīs reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
… [as before] … “Is it true, bhikkhus, that the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, having requested one thing, requests another?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, having requested one thing, request another?
This, bhikkhus, is neither for the pleasing of those without confidence nor for the increase of those with confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, the bhikkhunīs should recite this training rule thus:
“Whichever bhikkhunī, having requested one thing, should request another, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). Whichever bhikkhunī...
[means]... “whichever.”
Whichever [nun] of such a kind... "a nun" ...pe...
this is the nun intended in this context.
"Having requested something else" means having requested anything whatsoever.
"One might request something else" means...
If, setting that aside, she asks for something else, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of requesting.
Upon obtaining it, it becomes an article to be relinquished (nissaggiya).
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, a group, or a single bhikkhunī.
And thus, monks, it should be relinquished:
“… ‘Venerable ladies, this other thing which I requested after having already requested another is to be relinquished; I relinquish it to the Saṅgha. …pe…
“May she give,” … “May they give,” … “I give to the noble lady.”
If one asks for something else while perceiving another thing as such, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one asks for something else while being in doubt, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one asks for something else while perceiving it not as another thing, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it is not another person, but she perceives them as another and informs them that it is another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is not another person, but she is in doubt and informs them that it is another, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not another person and she does not perceive them as another, there is no offense.
There is no offense if she requests that very same thing, requests something else,
or requests it after pointing out its benefits.
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of one who is a first-offender.
The fourth training rule is concluded.
